findings.markdown:
**The proposed probability dynamics omit selected-action update frequencies and therefore do not model the traditional or lenient Q-learners used in the paper's central comparison.**

**Exact location.** PDF pages 4–5 (printed 426–427), Section 2.1.2's selected-action Q-learning update and Boltzmann policy; PDF page 10 (printed 432), Equation (13); PDF page 11 (printed 433), Equations (14)–(17); PDF pages 28–30 (printed 450–452), Equations (36)–(39), Section 5 and Figures 5–6; PDF pages 31–32 (printed 453–454), Figures 7–8 and the comparative conclusion. The abstract on PDF page 1 expressly advertises models for traditional multiagent Q-learning and the conclusion that algorithm choice has little effect relative to lenience.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** The paper describes a learner that chooses one action by its Boltzmann probabilities and updates that action's Q-value from the resulting reward. Its proposed continuous-time model is asserted to describe that learner and, after replacing expected rewards by expected maxima, its lenient version. Section 5 treats N=1 as traditional Q-learning and compares its policy-space attraction basins with those of CCEA. The counterexample uses two agents, two actions, one stateless common-payoff game, independent Boltzmann action choices, positive temperature, learning rate .1 and discount factor 0. These meet the stated setting. No full-information virtual updates or inverse-frequency learning-rate normalization is prescribed in Sections 2.1.2, 2.3.2 or 5.

**Error.** For a small physical time step delta, write the actual selected-action update as

\[
 \Delta Q_i=\alpha\delta\,\mathbf1\{I=i\}
       (A_{iJ}+\gamma\max_k Q_k-Q_i).
\]

Conditional expectation given the current Q-values and policies gives the mean drift

\[
 \dot Q_i=\alpha x_i\bigl(u_i+\gamma\max_k Q_k-Q_i\bigr),
 \qquad u_i=\sum_j A_{ij}y_j.
\tag{A}
\]

Equation (13) omits x_i. Differentiating the Boltzmann map correctly, as in Equation (12), therefore gives the actual small-step policy drift

\[
 \dot x_i=\frac{\alpha x_i}{\tau}\left[
 x_i\bigl(u_i+\gamma\max Q-Q_i\bigr)
 -\sum_k x_k^2\bigl(u_k+\gamma\max Q-Q_k\bigr)\right].
\tag{B}
\]

In particular this is generally not an autonomous function of x and y. The paper's entropy-plus-replicator equations follow from simultaneous action-value updates, which are a different learning process.

**Exact counterexample: the same predicted equilibrium has opposite actual drifts.** Take

\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \alpha=\frac1{10},\qquad\gamma=0,\qquad
 \tau=\frac1{4\log3}.
\]

Both agents have Q-values

\[
 Q^{(c)}=\left(\frac12+c,\frac34+c\right),
 \qquad c\in\{-1/10,0,1/10\}.
\]

Every one of these valid initializations has exactly the same Boltzmann policy

\[
 x=y=(1/4,3/4),
\]

and the same mean rewards u=(1/2,3/4). The game has a unique global optimum at joint action (1,1). For both agents, the right side of the paper's Equation (16) is exactly zero: the reward difference is -1/4, equal to tau times log(x_1/x_2). Thus the proposed model predicts a fixed policy for all three initializations.

Actual selected-action updating instead gives

\[
 \dot Q_1=-\alpha c/4,\quad
 \dot Q_2=-3\alpha c/4,\quad
 \boxed{\dot x_1=\frac{3\alpha c}{32\tau}}.
\]

For c=-.1 and c=.1 the respective drifts are

\[
 -0.0041197960825054113427\ldots,
 \qquad +0.0041197960825054113427\ldots,
\]

while the paper predicts zero. This discrepancy survives the small-step limit; it is not Jensen error from replacing the expectation of a nonlinear finite-step policy update. No scalar time change maps a zero predicted drift to these nonzero, opposite drifts.

More generally, changing all Q-values by c leaves a Boltzmann policy unchanged but changes the actual drift by

\[
 \Delta\dot x_i=-\frac{\alpha(1-\gamma)c}{\tau}
       x_i\left(x_i-\sum_k x_k^2\right).
\]

Thus the loss of state information is not confined to this single equilibrium: for a two-action nonuniform policy and gamma<1 the drift can be changed in either direction by its Q offset. Fixing an initial Q normalization would also need to track its subsequent evolution; it does not close the asserted policy-only differential equations.

**Reproducible evidence.** check.py derives the displayed formula numerically at 90-digit precision and independently enumerates all four possible joint actions. For delta=10^-2 through 10^-12 it computes the exact conditional expected policy increment divided by delta; these approach the nonzero values above, verifying the small-step interpretation directly. results.json records the values. The script also checks Theorem 1's expected-maximum formula against 50 exhaustive rational examples with ties, N=1 through 5; all pass.

As an illustrative additional check only, high-accuracy integration of the actual symmetric Q-mean ODE from these three initializations reaches policies approximately (.01483,.98517), (.25,.75), and (.99924,.000761) at time 4000. These numerical endpoints are not used as a proof of finite-step stochastic convergence probabilities; the exact drift and nonclosure contradiction do not depend on them.

**Primary-source corroboration and scope recheck.** The original official PDF matches the audited file. Its official landing page provides no correction or supplementary implementation. A later primary paper, [Kaisers and Tuyls, Frequency Adjusted Multi-agent Q-learning (AAMAS 2010), Section 3.1](https://michaelkaisers.com/publications/2010_AAMAS_MKaisers.pdf), derives the missing frequency factor and distinguishes standard Q-learning from the frequency-adjusted learner that obeys the model. A directly relevant primary follow-up, [Bloembergen, Kaisers and Tuyls, Lenient Frequency Adjusted Q-learning (BNAIC 2010), Sections 3–3.2](https://michaelkaisers.com/publications/2010_BNAIC_Bloembergen_LFAQ.pdf), explicitly cites this 2008 paper as reference [8], explains its simultaneous-update assumption, and introduces a different lenient learner to match its predictions. These later works corroborate the independent calculation; the error is established from the 2008 update rule itself.

**Reason for rejection.** This invalidates an expressly central modeling and comparative contribution, rather than an optional notation or rate constant: Figures 5–8 and the claim that CCEA and traditional multiagent Q-learning have nearly the same lenience-dependent basins are based on dynamics that cannot describe the stated Q-learning algorithm even at their purported fixed policies. Their input, an initial policy, omits state that changes the true drift. To retain traditional Q-learning, one must derive and analyze an enlarged Q-state process and recalculate the attraction comparisons, including the effect of lenient reward-collection schedules. Alternatively, inverse-frequency updates or simultaneous full-information updates change the learning algorithm to a different one; simply relabeling those results does not preserve the paper's advertised comparison with traditional Q-learning. The later frequency-adjusted variants make this distinction explicit.

The expected-maximum identity and the independent CCEA convergence result are not refuted. The report does not claim that lenience can never help ordinary Q-learning, that every plotted color is wrong, or that historical code or empirical learner runs fabricated any result. The specific error is the false identification underlying the central Q-learning dynamics and cross-algorithm conclusion.

**Discovery method.** Traced the described action-selection/update rule through the derivation of Equation (13), then tested whether the proposed policy-only state could represent all valid Q initializations.

**Verification method.** Independently conditioned the selected-action update to derive (A), differentiated the Boltzmann map to derive (B), constructed an exact same-policy counterexample, enumerated all finite joint outcomes in the small-step limit, rechecked original rendered pages 4–5, 10–11 and 28–32, and located two directly relevant primary follow-ups. Root independently read original PDF pages 1, 4–5, 8–11 and 28–32, inspected rendered pages 4, 10 and 28, symbolically re-derived the drift as 3 c log(3)/80, and independently enumerated all four joint outcomes at 70-digit precision. The targeted verification and results are saved as root-targeted-verification.md and root-targeted-verification.json; this is a targeted independent check, not a second full-paper review.

**Confidence.** High. The omitted factor follows directly from the selected-action indicator, and the exact zero-versus-opposite-drift witness satisfies the paper's stateless common-payoff setting. The rejection rationale is limited to the advertised traditional-Q-learning and comparative-basins contribution.

\[ Q^{(c)}=\left(\frac12+c,\frac34+c\right), \qquad c\in\{-1/10,0,1/10\}. \]

Every one of these valid initializations has exactly the same Boltzmann policy

\[ x=y=(1/4,3/4), \]

and the same mean rewards u=(1/2,3/4). The game has a unique global optimum at joint action (1,1). For both agents, the right side of the paper's Equation (16) is exactly zero: the reward difference is -1/4, equal to tau times log(x_1/x_2). Thus the proposed model predicts a fixed policy for all three initializations.

Actual selected-action updating instead gives

\[ \dot Q_1=-\alpha c/4,\quad \dot Q_2=-3\alpha c/4,\quad \boxed{\dot x_1=\frac{3\alpha c}{32\tau}}. \]

For c=-.1 and c=.1 the respective drifts are

\[ -0.0041197960825054113427\ldots, \qquad +0.0041197960825054113427\ldots, \]

while the paper predicts zero. This discrepancy survives the small-step limit; it is not Jensen error from replacing the expectation of a nonlinear finite-step policy update. No scalar time change maps a zero predicted drift to these nonzero, opposite drifts.

More generally, changing all Q-values by c leaves a Boltzmann policy unchanged but changes the actual drift by

\[ \Delta\dot x_i=-\frac{\alpha(1-\gamma)c}{\tau} x_i\left(x_i-\sum_k x_k^2\right). \]

Thus the loss of state information is not confined to this single equilibrium: for a two-action nonuniform policy and gamma<1 the drift can be changed in either direction by its Q offset. Fixing an initial Q normalization would also need to track its subsequent evolution; it does not close the asserted policy-only differential equations.

Reproducible evidence.

check.py derives the displayed formula numerically at 90-digit precision and independently enumerates all four possible joint actions. For delta=10^-2 through 10^-12 it computes the exact conditional expected policy increment divided by delta; these approach the nonzero values above, verifying the small-step interpretation directly. results.json records the values. The script also checks Theorem 1's expected-maximum formula against 50 exhaustive rational examples with ties, N=1 through 5; all pass.

As an illustrative additional check only, high-accuracy integration of the actual symmetric Q-mean ODE from these three initializations reaches policies approximately (.01483,.98517), (.25,.75), and (.99924,.000761) at time 4000. These numerical endpoints are not used as a proof of finite-step stochastic convergence probabilities; the exact drift and nonclosure contradiction do not depend on them.

Primary-source corroboration and scope recheck. The original official PDF matches the audited file. Its official landing page provides no correction or supplementary implementation. A later primary paper, Kaisers and Tuyls, Frequency Adjusted Multi-agent Q-learning (AAMAS 2010), Section 3.1, derives the missing frequency factor and distinguishes standard Q-learning from the frequency-adjusted learner that obeys the model. A directly relevant primary follow-up, Bloembergen, Kaisers and Tuyls, Lenient Frequency Adjusted Q-learning (BNAIC 2010), Sections 3–3.2, explicitly cites this 2008 paper as reference [8], explains its simultaneous-update assumption, and introduces a different lenient learner to match its predictions. These later works corroborate the independent calculation; the error is established from the 2008 update rule itself.

Reason for rejection.

This invalidates an expressly central modeling and comparative contribution, rather than an optional notation or rate constant: Figures 5–8 and the claim that CCEA and traditional multiagent Q-learning have nearly the same lenience-dependent basins are based on dynamics that cannot describe the stated Q-learning algorithm even at their purported fixed policies. Their input, an initial policy, omits state that changes the true drift. To retain traditional Q-learning, one must derive and analyze an enlarged Q-state process and recalculate the attraction comparisons, including the effect of lenient reward-collection schedules. Alternatively, inverse-frequency updates or simultaneous full-information updates change the learning algorithm to a different one; simply relabeling those results does not preserve the paper's advertised comparison with traditional Q-learning. The later frequency-adjusted variants make this distinction explicit.

The expected-maximum identity and the independent CCEA convergence result are not refuted. The report does not claim that lenience can never help ordinary Q-learning, that every plotted color is wrong, or that historical code or empirical learner runs fabricated any result. The specific error is the false identification underlying the central Q-learning dynamics and cross-algorithm conclusion.

Discovery method.

Traced the described action-selection/update rule through the derivation of Equation (13), then tested whether the proposed policy-only state could represent all valid Q initializations.

Verification method.

Independently conditioned the selected-action update to derive (A), differentiated the Boltzmann map to derive (B), constructed an exact same-policy counterexample, enumerated all finite joint outcomes in the small-step limit, rechecked original rendered pages 4–5, 10–11 and 28–32, and located two directly relevant primary follow-ups. Confidence.

High. The omitted factor follows directly from the selected-action indicator, and the exact zero-versus-opposite-drift witness satisfies the paper's stateless common-payoff setting. The rejection rationale is limited to the advertised traditional-Q-learning and comparative-basins contribution.

findings.title: The controlled gene-experiment posterior omits a model-dependent Jacobian
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2008__accepted__v9-seeger08a-01 — The controlled gene-experiment posterior omits a model-dependent Jacobian
findings.markdown:
### Exact location, affected claim, and assumptions

Original PDF page 7 (printed page 765), Section 2.2 and Equation (3), specifies a controlled system, with constant externally chosen disturbance u and observed steady-state difference x. It assumes a Gaussian residual with covariance σ²I and then treats u as a Gaussian response conditional on x. The displayed posterior is claimed to factor over rows of A into independent sparse regressions.

Original PDF page 20 (printed page 778), Section 4, emphasizes that for gene experiments **x is unknown and u is chosen**. It explicitly samples the predictive outcome by drawing A and then x = A^(−1)(u−ε), ε∼N(0,σ²I). The subsequent information-gain calculation sums rowwise relative entropies using the factorization from page 7.

Original PDF pages 26–28 describe the principal gene-network experiment and Figure 2, including the interpretation of posterior edge probabilities, synthetic stable nonlinear networks, 100 repetitions, a Laplace prior, fractional EP, and comparison of designed versus random experiments. The abstract and conclusion identify this as the main experimental demonstration of the framework. No claim below asserts these historical curves are empirically wrong.

### Error and exact evidence

For the explicitly sampled experiment x=A^(−1)(u−ε), the change of variables ε=u−Ax has absolute Jacobian |det A|. Thus the density of the *observed outcome* is

    p(x | u,A) = |det A| N(u | Ax,σ²I).

For m independent controlled experiments, the posterior is proportional to

    |det A|^m P(A) ∏_j N(u_j | Ax_j,σ²I).

The printed gene posterior omits |det A|^m. This factor depends on the unknown model and cannot be removed as a data-only constant. It couples the rows of A, so the supposed exact reduction to n independent sparse linear models is false for this experiment. This issue precedes any Gaussian/EP approximation.

A stable two-gene local witness is

    A = [[−1,1/4],[1/4,−1]], eigenvalues −5/4 and −3/4.

On its stable nonsingular neighborhood, log det A has mixed derivative

    ∂² log det A / (∂A_12 ∂A_21) = −256/225.

The independent Laplace prior and the printed rowwise Gaussian residual likelihood have zero mixed derivative between those two different rows and cannot cancel the missing term. This demonstrates failure on a regular stable region, rather than relying on singular matrices or an instability of the underlying dynamics.

### Consequence even with exact inference

In one dimension take the true stable coefficient a₀=−1, fixed control u=1 and σ=1. Then x=ε−1, E[x]=−1 and E[x²]=2. The printed per-observation population log target is, up to a constant,

    −(1+2a+2a²)/2,

whose maximum is a=−1/2. The correct target adds log|a| and has its stable negative maximum at a=−1. Any fixed proper Laplace prior vanishes after division of the log posterior by m, so this discrepancy persists with arbitrarily much data even if the inference approximation is exact. Fresh repeated-experiment numerical fits corroborate these exact population maximizers.

The uncertainty discrepancy is also exact at finite data. For a single outcome x=0 with u=1, σ=1 and a unit Laplace prior, the printed posterior is the unit Laplace density, with variance 2 and mode 0. The correct posterior is |a|exp(−|a|)/2, with variance 6 and modes ±1. This is a density-value calculation at a particular observed value; it does not claim the singleton x=0 has positive probability. Direct integration at x=±0.01 and ±0.1 confirms that the discrepancy persists on open outcome neighborhoods, which have positive probability under the specified experiment.

### Reason for rejection and limits

This is not a missing constant in EP, a routine quadrature correction, or an objection that approximate inference is imperfect. Including the determinant changes the inference problem: the rows are coupled and the unnormalized posterior is not generally log-concave on all matrices. The separable sparse-regression machinery and simple sum-of-row information score no longer constitute the asserted Bayesian posterior/design calculation for controlled gene outcomes. A different coupled approximation or an explicit conditional-regression/pseudolikelihood interpretation would be required. That is a substantive change to a prominently advertised application, although the core fixed-design sparse regression/EP algorithm and the image/compressive-sensing applications survive.

Conversely, the paper is candid that its design score is heuristic, with no useful approximation guarantee (PDF page 20), and that simulations violate an idealized Gaussian linear model. The implementation may still work empirically as a regression heuristic. No invalid historical ranking or claimed numerical savings is inferred solely from the model error. The withdrawn Bayesian interpretation is central to this application: the model is said to reduce exactly to independent sparse regressions before EP is introduced. Restoring that reduction requires changing the observation model, or replacing the method with coupled matrix inference. Neither is a correction of an EP constant or index. The conditional regression remains a possible heuristic, but is not the claimed posterior for the controlled experiment.

The original cited Steinke–Seeger–Tsuda 2007 primary application paper was checked for a rescue: it makes the same conditional-regression/factorization claim and does not supply the determinant. The original package URL currently returns 404. A newer author EP repository was inspected but is not the historical gene application driver. Neither a failed artifact search nor absent source is counted as evidence of an error.

### Reproduction and original evidence

`gene-likelihood-check.py` independently computes the symbolic stable-region derivative, exact population targets, high-precision finite posterior moments, and fresh finite-data targets. Its output is `gene-likelihood-results.json` and `gene-likelihood-output.txt`.  All 55 page renders and extracted full text are preserved in the standard audit locations.

### Discovery method

While tracing Section 2.2 into the sequential design procedure, I compared the declared controlled variables with the explicit predictive sampler on PDF page 20. Applying the change-of-variables formula exposed the omitted determinant; symbolic differentiation and a scalar population model then established its consequence.

### Verification method

The original rendered PDF pages 7 and 20 were inspected, and all 55 pages and Appendices A–E were checked for a different model or a stated working-likelihood convention. The executable check independently derives the determinant and stable mixed derivative, integrates posterior moments at 60-digit precision, and computes exact population maximizers. Parent root independently read the critical original sections and renders, verified density normalization by 60-digit integration, and rederived the symbolic derivative and population maxima. Its targeted review is preserved separately; it is not represented as a second full-paper review. Independent core tests also confirm the fixed-design EP gradients and matrix formulas, which narrows the finding.

### Confidence

**High.** The likelihood normalization, stable cross-row derivative, and asymptotic scalar discrepancy are exact consequences of the stated outcome sampler. Independent verification confirms the original scope and mathematics. The finding does not establish that any historical simulation score is wrong.
